rv.q: This is a Rolls Royce of a revival, precision-tooled and carrying the weight of the show's history lightly.
Three hours fly by as Hadden-Paton's Higgins and his chum Colonel Pickering turn Amara Okereke's Eliza into a lady.
It's witty and intelligent, but ever so slightly staid.
This is a very decent, very stylish, eventually quite audacious My Fair Lady. Not, though, a great one.
Bartlett Sher's timid production, first seen in New York four years ago, will make them merely smile and shuffle.
While there's plenty to recommend it, there are elements of this production that feel underpowered.
Fresh from Broadway, Bartlett Sher's production is slick and accomplished, but loses the narrative's subtlety in a crowd-pleasing burst of top-hatted kitsch.
Almost everything else, unfortunately, is problematic.
This is a thoughtful grappling with a rich and complex musical, balancing old-fashioned charm with fresh ideas, and, at its best, blossoming into a truly loverly night out.
It is all part of the theatricality that drives this production of what must be the most English of American musicals.

What truly saves it, and has lingered with me since, is the defiant, almost ethereal look on Eliza's face during the closing moments of Sher's revisionist twist on the original musical's somewhat controversial ending.
Seasoned theatregoers will, I suspect, have seen more pleasurable productions before. That doesn't stop this one from being a decent night out.
There's much to enjoy in My Fair Lady, including a lovely cameo from Dame Vanessa Redgrave. But whilst many scenes delight, the end result doesn't deliver a strong or engaged narrative.
Amara Okereke blossoms in the role of Eliza, from humble flower girl to debutante, Okereke's performance is flawless and utterly captivating.
Based on the experience, it's a solid three stars, but assuming technical issues are already sorted it should handsomely and happily soar to something rather 'loverly.'
